title: Definitions
text:
• Energy carriers are substances, impulses, radiation, or fields,
which contain or transmit energy – more precisely: from which
directly or through one or more conversions “usable” energy
can be obtained.
• An energy source is considered a system that "provides" the
energy.

title: Definitions
text:
•
Primary energy carriers occur naturally, such as coal, lignite, crude oil, or natural
gas, as well as renewable energy sources. They are not subjected to any
conversion.
•
In most cases, primary energy must be converted into secondary energy carriers
in power plants, refineries, etc. Secondary energy is the result of a conversion
process and is obtained with energy losses from primary energy (e.g., coke,
briquettes, electricity, district heating, heating oil, or gasoline).
•
End energy carriers are carriers of the energy consumed by the user (end energy),
which corresponds to secondary or primary energy reduced by conversion and
distribution losses.
•
Usable energy is the energy that is available after the final conversion in the
devices of the end consumer (e.g., light).

title: Economies of Scale
text:
Economies of scale" refers to the cost advantages that a business
can achieve as a result of an increase in its level of production or
output.
(In simpler terms, as a company grows and produces more units of a good or service, the
average cost of production per unit tends to decrease.)
There are two main types of economies of scale:
Internal Economies of Scale: These result from factors within the firm, such as
increased specialization, improved technology, better utilization of resources, and increased
bargaining power with suppliers.
External Economies of Scale: These occur outside the firm and are often industry-
specific. For example, a whole industry may benefit from a skilled labor force or improved
infrastructure in a particular region.

text:
Economies of scope
Economies of scope refers to the cost advantages that a
business can achieve by producing a variety of goods or
services rather than specializing in the production of a
single good or service. In other words, economies of scope
arise when the combined production of multiple products
results in lower average costs than producing each product
independently.
Economies of scope can result from shared production
processes, distribution channels, marketing effort, or
research and development.
Quelle: http://www.forschungsinformationssystem.de/servlet/is/409442/

title: Economies of scope
text:
• Diversification: Businesses that diversify their product or service
offerings may benefit from economies of scope. This
diversification can lead to shared resources and capabilities that
reduce overall production costs.
• Efficiency Gains: By leveraging common resources, such as
production facilities or distribution networks, a company can
achieve efficiency gains that contribute to cost savings.
• Risk Reduction: Diversifying the product or service portfolio can
also help spread business risk. If one product faces challenges, the
overall impact on the company may be mitigated by the success of
other products.
Quelle: http://www.forschungsinformationssystem.de/servlet/is/409442/

title: Economies of scope vs. Economies of Scale
text:
Economies of scope are often contrasted with economies of scale.
While economies of scale focus on cost reductions associated with
increased production of a single product, economies of scope focus
on cost advantages achieved through the joint production of multiple
products or services. Both concepts contribute to a firm's overall
efficiency and competitiveness.

title: Definition Critical Infrastructure (in Germany)
text:
•
The definition of critical infrastructure in Germany is outlined in the BSI
KritisV (Ordinance for Determining Critical Infrastructures). According to
this regulation, critical infrastructures (KRITIS) are organizations and
facilities of major importance for society, such as those in the energy,
information technology, telecommunications, transport, health, water,
finance, and other sectors. The failure or impairment of these
infrastructures would lead to sustained shortages of supplies, significant
disruptions to public order, safety and security, or other dramatic
consequences.
•
The BSI KritisV sets qualitative and quantitative criteria to determine which infrastructures
are considered critical, including those in the energy sector. For example, the thresholds for
power plants to be considered critical infrastructure were lowered from 420 megawatts to
104 megawatts as of January 1, 2022.

title: Storage
text:
"Storage" = Space where objects are placed during times when
they are not directly or immediately used or needed = (quasi-)
permanent confining of goods or items, including (easily
accessible) input and output.
While transport refers to the movement of objects in space, storage (abstractly) can be
described as the movement of objects in time.
For transport, an "object" is simultaneously "fed in" at the transfer point and
“withdrawn" at the receiving point,
while in (physical) storage, an object is "input" at one point in time and "output" at a
later point in time—typically at the same location.

A graph (sometimes called an undirected graph to distinguish it

title: Sub-additive Cost Function
text:
A cost function is sub-additive if the total cost of producing the
combined output of two or more processes is less than or equal to
the sum of the costs of producing each output separately.
Let C(x) be the cost function associated with producing output x,
where x can represent various units of production.
The cost function is sub-additive if, for any two outputs a and b:
C(a+b)≤C(a)+C(b)
This implies that the cost of producing both a and b together is not greater than the sum of the costs of
producing each separately. Sub-additivity often reflects economies of scale or synergies in production
processes. When a cost function is sub-additive, it suggests that combining production activities can
result in cost savings compared to producing the same outputs independently. Thus, sub-additivity
indicates efficiency gains when resources are used in combination.

title: Natural Monopoly: Characteristics
text:
Economies of Scale (only a sufficient but not necessary condition in the single-product case
for subadditivity)
Economies of Scope (not sufficient for subadditivity)
Network effects
High fixed costs (investment, sunk costs)
(often) high demand for standardization
Potential competitor has no interest in market entry
No artificial barriers to market entry necessary
Indivisibilities, so that capacities can only be expanded in discrete increments
(density and bundling effects)
Instability of the natural monopoly possible for submarkets

• Natural Monopoly
• Vulnerability of a Market
The vulnerability of a market, i.e., the potential entry of new companies, is particularly
determined by irreversible costs (sunk cost), cost differences due to learning effects,
technological advantages, etc., information asymmetries, and the willingness of customers to
switch, which may be influenced by brand names, or long-term contracts with a provider.
• Essential Facility
An facility is considered essential when it is indispensable for reaching customers and/or enabling
competitors to conduct their business, not otherwise available in the market, or objectively
cannot be reasonably created anew with economic means.

text:

telecommunications regulation. ⇒Risk of overregulation

text:
"Storage" = Space where objects are placed during times when
they are not directly or immediately used or needed = (quasi-)
permanent confining of goods or items, including (easily

described as the movement of objects in time.
For transport, an "object" is simultaneously "fed in" at the transfer point and
“withdrawn" at the receiving point,
while in (physical) storage, an object is "input" at one point in time and "output" at a
later point in time—typically at the same location.

Purpose

(title) of a specific quantity of

buyer at a designated point.

point to an exit point within a
transmission system.
To provide a service for storing
a shipper's gas in a storage
facility over a specified period.

large portfolio company. Buyer:
Utility, industrial consumer, or
trader.
Shipper: The party (e.g., a
utility, trader, or industrial
consumer) that holds title to the
gas. Transporter: The
Transmission System Operator
(TSO) that owns and operates
the pipeline network.
Customer/Shipper: The party
(e.g., a utility or trader) that
holds title to the gas. Storage
Operator: The company that
owns and operates the storage
facility (Storage System
Operator (SSO)).
Subject of Agreement
Quantity
The sale and purchase of a
specified quantity of natural gas.
This is a transfer of a physical
commodity.
Capacity between entry and
exit
The right to use capacity in a
pipeline network for the
transportation of natural gas.
Working gas capacity,
injection rate, withdrawal rate

text:
Paragraph
Natural Gas Commodity
Import Contract (e.g., Long-
Term GSPA)
Natural Gas Transportation
Contract (GTA)
Natural Gas Storage Contract
Term
Long-term contracts can span
from 10 to 25+ years (include
inter alia price renegotiation)
Short term contract (mostly
hubs)
The term can vary widely, from
short-term (e.g., one day) to
medium-term (e.g., one year)
and occasionally longer.
The term is typically annual,
designed to cover a full cycle of
injections (summer) and
withdrawals (winter). Shorter-term
products may also be available.
Quantity
Specifies the Contract Quantity
(e.g., a total volume over the term of
the contract) and often includes
Daily Contract Quantity (DCQ),
Annual Contract Quantity
(ACQ), and provisions for
flexibility (take-or-pay or deliver-
or-pay). (Mostly [Wh], [BTU], or
[m³])
Defines Reserved Capacity or
Maximum Daily Quantity (MDQ)
in energy units (e.g., kWh/day
or MMBtu/day) that the shipper
can use.
Defines a total Working Gas
Volume (maximum inventory)
and daily limits for Maximum
Injection Capacity (MIC) and
Maximum Withdrawal
Capacity (MWC). ([m³] or [Wh]
and [m³/h] or[W] for the latter
two)
Price
The price of the gas commodity
itself. Historically indexed to oil
prices, but today also linked to
a natural gas trading hub price
(e.g., TTF, NBP). May include
formulas, floors, and caps.
Transmission Charges (tariffs)
for the service of transportation.
These are typically fixed
capacity charges and/or
variable commodity charges,
regulated/approved by national
authorities.
Storage Fees or Tariffs for the
storage service. These are
often a mix of capacity fees (for
the right to store) and variable
fees (for injections and
withdrawals), subject to
regulatory oversight.

Delivery Point: The specific
point where the legal title and
risk of the gas transfer from

physical interconnection point.
Entry Point: Where the
shipper's gas enters the
pipeline system. Exit Point:
Where the shipper's gas is
redelivered from the system.
Injection Point: Where the gas
is put into storage from the

Withdrawal Point: Where the

returned to the transmission
system.

Governs how the buyer
nominates the amount of gas
they wish to take on a daily
basis within the agreed-upon
flexible limits. (Frequently, also
indicative nominations for
longer periods.)
The shipper must submit daily
nominations to the TSO,
detailing the quantity of gas to
be transported each day from
the entry to the exit point.
The customer must submit
nominations to the storage
operator for daily injection or
withdrawal quantities.

title: German Storage Law I
text:
•
The law introducing filling level specifications for natural gas storages
came into force on May 1st, 2022.
•
If not done by private companies, Trading Hub Europe GmbH (market area
manager/operator) is
obliged to fill the natural gas storage facilities (§ 35b EnWG / EU-VO 2022/10321):
by November 1st: 90% and by February 1st: 45%; additionally figures for summer
months defined
•
Planned multi-stage procedure incentivizing storage filling; main elements:
– Tenders to establish base provision (SSBO: Strategic Storage Based Options)
– If the storage is not sufficiently filled, the market area manager can auction
capacities
– Unused capacities must be returned to the market area manager, who will also
buy natural gas to fill them

title: Key Elements of a Crude Oil Shipping Contract
text:
1. Contract Types
1. Voyage Charter: The shipowner agrees to transport crude oil from one
port to another for a fixed freight rate.
2. Time Charter: The charterer hires the vessel for a set period, paying
daily hire rates.
3. Bareboat Charter: The charterer takes full control of the vessel,
including crewing and operations.
2. Incoterms (International Commercial Terms)
1. FOB (Free on Board): Seller delivers oil onto the vessel; buyer assumes
risk and costs thereafter.
2. CFR (Cost and Freight): Seller pays freight to destination port but risk
transfers once oil is loaded.
3. CIF (Cost, Insurance, Freight): Seller covers freight and insurance to
destination port.

part: Oil and Oil Product Transport and Storage
title: Key Elements of a Crude Oil Shipping Contract
text:
3. Freight Rate System
Contracts often reference the AFRA system (Average Freight Rate
Assessment), which classifies tanker sizes (e.g., Aframax, Suezmax, VLCC,
ULCC) and sets standardized freight rates.
4. Technical & Operational Clauses
1. Vessel specifications (capacity, safety standards, classification society
approval).
2. Loading/discharge port details and laytime (time allowed for
loading/unloading).
3. Demurrage (penalty if loading/discharge exceeds agreed laytime).
4. Insurance and liability clauses (pollution, cargo loss, accidents).

part: Oil and Oil Product Transport and Storage
title: Key Elements of a Crude Oil Shipping Contract
text:
5. Risk & Responsibility
1. Clear definition of when risk passes from seller to buyer (usually when
crude is loaded on board).
2. Compliance with international maritime law (MARPOL, SOLAS) and
local port regulations.
6. Practical Considerations
1. Environmental & Safety Regulations: Contracts must comply with IMO
rules and oil pollution liability conventions.
2. Geopolitical Risks: Shipping routes often cross chokepoints (e.g., Strait
of Hormuz, Malacca Strait), so contracts may include force majeure
clauses.
3. Insurance: Marine insurance is critical, especially under CIF terms,
covering cargo loss, piracy, or accidents.

part: Introduction and overview of energy systems analysis
title: Steps of systems analysis (1)
text:
1. Formulate the problem:
Precisely identify and specify the problem (
Cook et al. 1985: „It’s difficult to
arrive at the right answer if you are working on the wrong problem”)
Define the target of the analysis
2. Define the system and its boundaries and choose a model type:
Define and describe the relevant parts/parameters as well as boundaries of
the system
Define the model type to be used for the analysis
3. Data collection:
Often the most time expensive step of modelling a system
Challenge: avoid collection of unessential
individual data, which increases
the complexity of the problem without contributing to better decision
support
Sometimes,
simplifications of reality are necessary on the input side of a
model in order to receive model output, which matches better with reality

part: Introduction and overview of energy systems analysis
title: Steps of systems analysis (2)
text:
4. Model development and implementation:
A realistic description of the functionality / cause effect relations within the
system is important in the modelling step
Challenge: restrict modelling to the system
characteristics, which are
essential to solve the problem (“Don’t model the whole world”)
Choose an appropriate software environment for the model implementation

part: Introduction and overview of energy systems analysis
title: Steps of systems analysis (3)
text:
5. Model validation:
Validation whether the essential cause effect relations are represented
correctly by the model
→ it can be efficient to carry out this validation on the basis of a small test
data set
Backtesting
the model on the basis of real (historical) system data
→ e.g. collect data about historical load/demand, fuel prices etc. from
official entities
Evaluation criterion: Can history be reconstructed / explained? How close
can history be constructed?
Quantitatively: Calculate mean
absolute, mean relative or mean quadratic
deviation between model results and officially published data (e.g.
generation balance, prices)

part: Introduction and overview of energy systems analysis
title: Steps of systems analysis (4)
text:
6. Model application: Use the model for scenario-based analyses of likely
developments of the energy system
Define the scenarios to be investigated
Identify crucial drivers and uncertainties
Carry out scenario calculations
Check the model results for plausibility
In case
of implausibilities, the scenario assumptions or the model itself
might need to be refined iteratively
7. Interpret results and draw conclusions
What do the model results mean for the decision to be taken?
Think about how the model results shall be used in the decision making
process
Think about how to handle uncertainties / differing results in different
scenarios

input, do not

Distinction of two basic situations
Enough capacity is available
If there is enough capacity, the suppliers make bids according to their

As target function of a systems model, the minimisation of the total
system’s costs under the hard constraint of load coverage is common
New capacity is needed

be chosen from a set of alternative options; typically ‘optimal’ means that
the expansion candidate is chosen which contributes to minimising the
system expenses →macroeconomic approach
Therefore, it cannot be concluded that the optimal expansion option from a
systems perspective will be economically profitable from an entrepreneurial

title: General Setup and methodology The supply curve
text:
How will a generator offer his electricity?
In
a competitive market a supplier adjusts his output until marginal
costs equal the market price.
Thus a price
-taker's supply curve and his marginal cost curve are the
same.
Therefore,
a supplier will offer his electricity at his marginal costs.
Many power markets rely on a central day
-ahead auction. Because
prices should equal marginal costs, the auctioning rules should be
informed by a coherent theory of marginal costs

part: Fundamental optimisation models (1): optimal unit commitment
title: Marginal costs of an individual generator vs. system marginal costs
text:
Marginal costs:
Marginal costs are the change in total costs that arise when the quantity
produced is incremented by one unit (e.g., MWh of electricity), i.e. at different
production levels, marginal costs include any additional costs required to
produce one more unit
Individual generator:
Marginal costs = costs for producing one more MWhel
→Assuming a constant efficiency, marginal costs of an individual generator
equal variable costs
System marginal costs:
Marginal costs = lowest costs for producing one more MWhel from the
perspective of the system
→Variable costs of the ‘cheapest’ generator that can produce one more unit
Beware:
In mixed integer linear programmes (MILPs), system marginal costs are often
≠ marginal costs of most expensive generator needed to cover demand

title: Uncertainty in short term dispatch: Modelling of outages using convolution (1)
text:
Real world technical appliances, like power plants, need maintenance
and fail from time to time
In hours where a plant is off
-line, it will not contribute to meet the load
this effect can be included in energy system analysis models
Obviously, the exact point in time, where failure occurs, is not known
beforehand …
… but the amount of hours is determined by probability, known from
historic track records
As an alternative method, Monte Carlo simulation can be applied, but
convolution provides a more precise result, as all possible
combinations are analysed
Optimal unit commitment
(short-term planning)

title: Uncertainty in short term dispatch:
text:
Uncertainty in short term dispatch: Modelling of outages using
convolution (2): Convolution “step by step”
The load duration curve is transformed to a shape with steps of
constant load
The power plant with the lowest cost is dispatched first
The basic assumption is, that outages might occur at any point in time
and are not related to a specific time/season
For those hours, where the plant is not available, the load is not met (or
graphically: not reduced). Other blocks need to cover the load in those
time slices
As the is a (very low) probability that all plants fail at the same time, the
load can never be met with a 100% certainty (no matter how many
blocks are in the system)
For modelling purposes the missing energy, which needs to be
procured externally, is allocated with a very high price

title: Fundamental optimisation models for power systems analysis Distinction of two basic …
text:
Fundamental optimisation models for power systems analysis
Distinction of two basic situations
Enough capacity is available
If there is enough
capacity, the suppliers make bids according to their
(short-run) marginal costs
As target function of a systems
model, the minimisation of the total
system’s costs under the hard constraint of load coverage is common
New capacity is needed
In the event that demand grows and/or old power plants reached the end of
their lifetime, new capacity may be needed
From a systems perspective, the ‘optimal’ capacity expansion option is to
be chosen from a set of alternative options; typically ‘optimal’ means that
the expansion candidate is chosen which contributes to minimising the
system expenses →macroeconomic approach
Therefore, it cannot be concluded that the optimal expansion option from a
systems perspective will be economically profitable from an entrepreneurial
perspective

In energy systems modelling, a distinction can be made between

Perfect-Foresight
All input assumptions over the whole horizon of calculation are known

Decision making in the energy sector typically involves a long

title: Source: based on Yoe et al. (2004)
text:
1) Decide on the key drivers for your scenarios. Determine the most important factors that will decide
the nature of the future environment. Brainstorm lists of drivers. Apply the 80:20 rule so managers
and others can focus on what is truly important. Look for drivers that are subject to significantly
different alternative futures, i.e., things that are important and uncertain.
5) Write the scenarios. Produce the scenarios in the form most suitable for use by planners and
managers who are going to use the scenarios to develop plans/strategies.
6) Identify issues arising. Examine the scenarios to identify the most critical outcomes and the issues
that will have the greatest impact on the future. The scenarios can then be used in planning.
4) Reduce scenarios. Reduce the mini scenarios to a few (3-5) larger scenarios. Experience suggests
managers encounter difficulties coping effectively with too many more than three scenarios.
2) Bring drivers together into a viable framework, i.e. it is necessary to link the critical drivers together
in a viable framework. Construct ‘event strings’ that link drivers so as to see the linkages and their
progression over time. Group drivers into combinations that are meaningful.
3) Construct ‘mini-scenarios’. Step 2) often produces 5-10 groups of drivers. Now it is time to work out
the connections among these groups. What does each group represent? Develop a mini-scenario
around each group of drivers.

title: Decision making in the energy sector The entrepreneurial perspective
text:
Main target of energy systems analysis: Generate a set of scenarios as
a framework to analyse chances and risks associated with strategic
decisions, e.g. to support the economic evaluation of investments
Consequence(s)
In the event that a decision is to be taken on an NPV basis, an investment
decision is represented by a bandwidth of NPVs – one fore each scenario
It is likely that an investment project achieves a positive NPV in one
scenario and a negative NPV in another one
The same holds true for other indicators (e.g. IRR etc.)
Central challenge(s)
How can the uncertainties (chances/risks) associated with an investment
decision be transported/communicated/visualised to the decision makers in
an understandable way?
How can/should the information on uncertainties associated with strategic
decisions be used in the decision making process, i.e. how should the
results be interpreted?

decision is listed
The
decision chosen is the one corresponding to the minimum of the
maximum regrets

title: Voltage levels Low voltage networks
text:
•
The majority of electrical consumers consist of low-voltage devices.
•
The final distribution of electrical energy to these consumers takes place via low-voltage
networks, which are fed via network stations from a higher-level medium-voltage network.
•
Rated power of the grid stations: 250 kVA, 400 kVA or 630 kVA
•
The structure of the networks depends largely on the load density parameter , which
indicates the sum of all loads based on the area.
Medium voltage networks
•
A medium-voltage network is fed from a high-voltage network via substations .
•
Rated power of the substations: 20 – 50 MVA
•
The medium-voltage network distributes the electrical energy via network stations to the
lower-level low-voltage networks.
•
The choice of nominal voltage depends on the load density.

section: Structure of the power grid and voltage levels
title: Voltage levels High and extra-high voltage networks
text:
•
The high-voltage networks are supplied to a small extent by individual medium- and peak-
load power plants, but predominantly by feed-ins from a high-voltage network, which are
referred to as substations .
•
Rated power of the substations: 100 – 300 MVA
•
High-voltage networks are pure transport networks that connect the power plants with the
substations and the transport network of your own company with those of its neighbors.
•
Despite its comparatively simple structure, the extra-high voltage network is particularly
safe.
•
Due to particularly intensive maintenance of the operating resources and a high degree of
automation in network operation management, the high-voltage network has a very high
level of availability.

• An electrical equipment, transformer, line or power plant may fail at any time without

• In a correctly operated system, at least two events must come together for supply
interruptions to occur
• Energy supply companies usually cite a defect in a power plant, damage to a line, a short

However, if the regulation works, these occasions would generally not be a reason for a
power outage.

title: Haber Bosch Process
text:
Developed by German chemists Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch in the first
decade of the 20th century
>90 % of global ammonia production by Haber-Bosch
Hydrogen and nitrogen are synthesized at temperatures of 400 – 450 °C
and pressures around 120 – 220 bar in the presence of an iron catalyst
N2 + 3 H2 →2 NH3
ΔH0 = -91.8 kJ/mol
exothermic, but energy required for compression
and activation energy/pre-heating
Low conversion (<20%) limited by thermodynamics, thereby requiring
condensation to remove ammonia before recompressing and feeding
unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen back to the reactor
For 1 kg NH3
(stoichiometric):
• 0.18 kg H2
• 0.82 kg N2

Non-toxic
Simple storage and transport as bulk material (TRL 8-9)
